purpose: Omalizumab is used to help control moderate to severe allergic asthma that is not well managed with inhaled steroids alone. It is also used to treat chronic hives (called chronic idiopathic urticaria) when antihistamines are not working well enough. In some cases, it may be used to help reduce allergic reactions in people with certain food allergies.
how_it_works: Your immune system makes a protein called IgE, which plays a big role in triggering allergic reactions like asthma attacks and hives. Omalizumab works by attaching to that IgE protein and blocking it before it can set off an allergic reaction. Think of it like putting a cap on the trigger so your body does not overreact to allergens as easily.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include pain, redness, bruising, or itching at the injection site. Some people experience headaches, tiredness, or a mild rash. You might also notice joint or muscle aches, especially when you first start the medication.
warnings: A serious but rare allergic reaction called anaphylaxis can happen, sometimes even hours after your injection, so your first few doses are given in a clinic where you can be monitored. Tell your doctor right away if you have trouble breathing, chest tightness, dizziness, or swelling of the throat or tongue after your injection. There is also a small potential increased risk of certain cancers, though this has not been clearly proven. Do not stop your other asthma medicines without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: Omalizumab is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection) every 2 to 4 weeks, depending on your body weight and your IgE level in the blood. Your doctor will calculate the right dose specifically for you. The first few doses are given in a doctor's office or clinic, and later doses may sometimes be given at home once your doctor says it is safe.
